title: How Paul wrote
hookLine: letters dictated to real churches with real problems, before the gospels were written

cards: A box of old family letters, found in an attic. Not speeches. Letters.

Answers to questions nobody wrote down, jokes that need context, names no one remembers, a worry about money, a fight between cousins, and then, in the middle of it all, a paragraph worth reading twice.
That's what i'm opening today: a new part of the path, the letters of the New Testament, and first, the letters of Paul.

teach.b: The word is epistle, from the Greek epistole: simply a letter, something sent.
First surprise: a common scholarly view places Paul's letters before the Gospels were written down.
On that view, opening Paul means hearing a voice from the first Christian generation, writing to churches that were still new. Second, Paul didn't always hold the pen.
At times he dictated to a secretary, and at the end of Romans the secretary slips in his own greeting. In the Douay-Rheims: "I Tertius, who wrote this epistle, salute you in the Lord."

teach.h: DICTATED, THEN SIGNED IN BIG LETTERS.
teach.b: In several letters Paul then takes the pen for the last lines, as a signature. To the Galatians: "See what a letter I have written to you with my own hand." The Greek speaks of large letters: big handwriting, his own.
Third, these were real letters to real people with real problems. Corinth is split into factions. The Galatians are confused.
The Thessalonians are grieving their dead. Paul answers them, scolds them, misses them, and greets friends by name.
The letters were carried by hand and read aloud to the whole church. A whole set of New Testament letters carries Paul's name.

Scholars debate whether he wrote every one or whether some come from his close followers; the Church receives all of them as scripture. At Sunday Mass, the second reading often comes from these letters.
You're hearing someone else's mail, and it was meant to be shared.

how: At Sunday Mass, Catholics usually hear three readings, and the second is most often from the New Testament letters, many of them Paul's; it is read aloud to the whole assembly, as the letters first were.

games.q: you're Paul. a church you started, far away, is fighting and confused, and you can't travel there. what do you do?
o: dictate a letter, sign it, and send it with a friend.
let them sort it out themselves.
games.why: that's how his letters came to be: real answers to real problems, carried by hand and read aloud.

practice: Think of someone you haven't really written to in a long time, and compose three sentences to them in your head, the kind that might be kept: thanks for something specific, a memory, or encouragement for something hard they're facing.
Imagine signing it in your own big letters. If you pray, pray for that person, as Paul so often did in his opening lines.
